title: Corvus the Brave Raven
markdown:
Misty Kettle Mountain always wore a soft grey mist, like a cozy wool blanket. After a good sprinkle the air smelled sweet, like blooming heather. On one gentle slope, in a cottage that looked built from warm gingerbread, lived Magnus. Hair the colour of sunshine on a dandelion puff. Eyes that sparkled with wonder, though curiosity sometimes outran bravery. His very best friend was a raven as black as the deepest night, eyes that twinkled with secrets. Magnus called him Corvus.

The Misty Kettle Mountain Festival was drawing near. Music, laughter, the most delightful berry tarts in all the land. The biggest prize, the one that made Magnus’s heart thump like a robin’s wings, was the Bravest Bloom ribbon, for the most astonishing display of magic. Magnus, who loved conjuring wonders, really wanted to win it this year.

“Just imagine, Corvus. The prettiest ribbon, all for the bravest spell. I’ll make flowers waltz and teach the wind to hum happy tunes.”

Corvus, perched on Magnus’s shoulder, tilted his glossy head and let out a soft rumbly caw. Magnus always understood this to mean: and will there be extra sunflower seeds for such a grand show?

Magnus’s special spell was the Sparkle Shower. A swish of a smooth willow wand, a few rhyming words, glittering dust falling, smelling a little of honey and moonlight. Lately it had been a bit wobbly. Sparkles tumbling too fast, or hanging too long. Once a whole cloud landed on Corvus’s beak, making him sneeze tiny sparkles for a whole minute. Magnus would let out a quiet sigh. “Oh dear,” smoothing dandelion-fluff hair.

One morning the mist was so thick it felt like walking through a fluffy cloud. “Today, Corvus, we shall explore the Whispering Woods. That’s where the most amazing Bravest Blooms are said to grow.”

Corvus stretched his wings, a faint flicker of excitement. Wonders. Perhaps crumbs.

The woods lived up to their name. Tall old trees whispered secrets, leaves rustling like pages in a forgotten book. Sunlight dappled, dancing spots on mossy ground. Deeper, Magnus felt that familiar flutter: part adventure, part a tiny whisper of worry. The woods so very big. Trees so high. A young wizard quite small.

A tiny clear voice chirped from beside a fern as big as Magnus’s favourite armchair. “Stop, travellers. Be careful. The emerald moss is slicker than a freshly polished river stone.”

Peeking from a velvety green frond: a tiny elf, no taller than Magnus’s knee, hair like spun cobwebs touched by morning dew, a tunic of forget-me-not petals. Elara. Gentle grace, tiny feet barely disturbing fallen leaves.

“Hello.” Magnus tried to sound like a seasoned explorer. “We are looking for the Bravest Bloom for the Mountain Festival.”

Elara nodded, bright eyes like tiny forest pools. “It does grow deep within these woods. Be watchful. Roots like sneaky ropes. Shadows that play tricks.” A slender finger. “And take care of the soft-pawed creatures that might be lurking.”

Magnus felt a little more sure-footed. Corvus was busy watching a plump shiny beetle on a fallen log.

They continued. Cooler air, damp soil, fragrant pine. Magnus laid out spell parts on welcoming moss: a pouch of shimmering moon-dust, a tiny cluster of whisper-grass seeds, three perfectly smooth grey river stones.

“Now, Corvus. Watch closely. This is how the Bravest Bloom truly begins to show its magic.”

He lifted the willow wand, took a deep steady breath, began to chant. Just as the rhyming words left his lips, a playful gust, faint scent of distant rain, swept the clearing. Hair against his face. Moon-dust swirled. Whisper-grass seeds took flight like tiny dancers. The three stones skittered under a tangle of prickly brambles.

Magnus gasped. Spell parts scattered. Tummy a flip-flop. A familiar prickle behind the eyes.

Then Corvus, who had been watching with his head tilted in that way he had, did not just stand by. A powerful determined beat of strong wings. He launched, swooped, dived, sleek black a swift blur against shifting sunlight. He snatched shimmering moon-dust in his beak, gathered dancing seeds with a precise peck, nudged a stray river stone from under the brambles with a skillful flick of his foot. Landed with a triumphant caw, a little ruffled, all the vital parts safely in his beak.

Elara, eyes as wide as saucers, let out a cascade of tinkling giggles, tiny silver bells. “Oh, Corvus. You are indeed brave. And just a little bit wonderfully messy.”

Magnus stared. His sometimes quiet raven, often more interested in a tasty snack than grand wizardry, had been utterly magnificently brave. Not afraid of the gust or the scattered magic. He had simply done what needed to be done.

Magnus looked at the parts in Corvus’s beak, at his own still slightly wobbly spell, at the tiny careful elf beaming at the raven. A different feeling bloomed, warm and strong. Pride, deep and true.

So Magnus and Corvus journeyed back to the festival, not with a perfect gleaming Sparkle Shower, but with a wonderful story that made everyone gathered chuckle and smile. Magnus didn’t win the Bravest Bloom ribbon for his spell that day. Instead the festival organiser, a kindly woman with cheeks as rosy as ripe apples, stepped forward.

“For the true spirit of adventure,” she announced, voice clear as a bluebird’s song, “and for the most unexpected hero of our day.” With a flourish she gently pinned a small shiny medal onto Corvus’s chest.

Corvus puffed out his chest feathers, preening with grand importance. Magnus stood proudly beside him, a wide happy smile. He had not won the ribbon. He had found a friend whose bravery he had never quite imagined, and a Sparkle Shower that could sneeze. As the sun dipped below the misty kettle, rose and gold, Magnus saved extra sunflower seeds. Corvus, medal glinting, did not sneeze this time. The beetle, if it had followed them home, kept its own counsel, which was how you knew a raven could be the bloom.
characters: Magnus (young wizard with dandelion-fluff hair), Corvus (a raven as black as the deepest night)
author: StoryGen Community
